text: Where churn asks which class, price prediction asks how much. The workflow is the same, but the details differ: regression metrics, a skewed target, and errors that grow with the price. This lesson predicts illustrative house prices end to end.

Three thousand illustrative homes, priced from about sixty-six thousand five hundred dollars to eight hundred six thousand, with a mean near two hundred seventy-nine thousand and a mild right skew of zero point five five. We'll judge models with mean absolute error, the average dollar miss, because it's easy to explain.

Predicting the mean price misses by about ninety-eight thousand dollars; that's the baseline to beat. Plain ridge regression cuts the error to thirty-one thousand two hundred seventy-seven. Gradient boosting does better still, twenty-nine thousand three hundred forty-six, and adding a log-transformed target brings it to twenty-eight thousand eight hundred thirty-two, the best of the five.

Notice the log target helped boosting slightly but actually hurt the ridge model. Always test a transformation; don't assume it helps. And because the fold-to-fold spread is only about seven hundred dollars, the gap among the top three candidates is modest.

On the held-out test set, the chosen model scores a mean absolute error of twenty-eight thousand nine hundred thirty-two dollars, a root mean squared error of forty thousand one hundred ninety-one, and an R-squared of point eight eight four. RMSE is larger than MAE because it punishes big misses harder.

The predicted-versus-actual plot hugs the diagonal, a good sign. But the residual plot shows a funnel: errors widen as price rises. The model is off by ten to twenty thousand dollars on cheaper homes, and fifty thousand or more on some expensive ones. Report that honestly.

Baseline first, test transformations rather than assuming them, and read the residual plot to find where the model is weakest. Next: fraud detection, where the imbalance from chapter four returns in a full project.
